name: Minoxidil
lead: Minoxidil, sold as Rogaine and Loniten among other brands, is a vasodilator medication used for high blood pressure and for hair loss. Taken orally at high doses it treats severe hypertension, while topical minoxidil, available over the counter as a solution or foam, is used for androgenetic alopecia, and low-dose oral minoxidil is prescribed off-label for hair loss.[1] Topical 2 percent solution and 5 percent solution and foam are FDA-approved for androgenetic alopecia, and oral minoxidil is not FDA-approved for hair loss.[2][3]

Wikipedia describes the drug as promoting hair growth, but its effects as fully reversible: benefits depend on indefinite use, and after long-term treatment is stopped hair density falls to placebo levels within about 24 weeks.[1] Meta-analyses of randomised trials found 2 percent and 5 percent topical minoxidil superior to placebo in men, and a 2024 randomised trial in JAMA Dermatology compared oral and topical minoxidil in men.[4][5][6]

Minoxidil acts independently of androgens, which is why it is frequently discussed alongside 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride.[7][8] Topical side effects are mainly scalp irritation, itching and unwanted hair growth elsewhere; oral minoxidil can cause fluid retention, rapid heartbeat, dizziness and hypertrichosis, and rare serious events such as pericardial effusion have been described mainly at higher doses.[1][7] Minoxidil is also reported to be hazardous if swallowed by children, with a published case of a child's accidental ingestion.[1]
infobox: Potassium channel opener, direct-acting vasodilator; prodrug of minoxidil sulfate

paras: Topical minoxidil in 5 percent foam, 5 percent solution and 2 percent solution is FDA-approved for androgenetic alopecia in men and women, per a comprehensive review.[2] Wikipedia states that its effectiveness has largely been demonstrated in younger men with hair loss of under five years, that it is less effective when the area of loss is large, and that the over-the-counter label indicates vertex hair loss only.[1] The US label for a 5 percent product states it is for men only, is not intended for frontal baldness or a receding hairline, and warns it is flammable.[10]

Low-dose oral minoxidil is used off-label for hair loss; Wikipedia says it is considered an alternative for those who have difficulty with topical formulations, and notes that almost all users of topical minoxidil discontinue within a year, according to the source it cites.[1] Higher oral doses were more effective for hair but caused more hypertrichosis.[1] Sublingual minoxidil is under study, and a phase 3 trial of sublingual tablets in men with androgenetic alopecia (NCT06924632) was listed as completed.[1][11]

Minoxidil has been studied for beard growth, including in transgender men, and for nail disorders in at least six clinical studies.[1] Registered trials have also tested it for endocrine therapy-induced alopecia in breast cancer, and oral minoxidil in recurrent ovarian cancer.[12][13] Wikipedia notes use for hypertension is reserved for severe cases not responding to at least two other agents plus a diuretic.[1]

A 48-week randomised double-blind trial in men compared 5 percent topical minoxidil, 2 percent minoxidil and placebo.[14] A comprehensive review states that in a five-year study 2 percent minoxidil reached peak growth in men at year one and declined after, and that 5 percent solution and foam did not differ significantly from 2 percent in efficacy.[2] The same review reported that after six months oral 5 mg per day was significantly more effective than topical 5 percent and 2 percent in male androgenetic alopecia, and that 0.5 to 5 mg per day may be effective for female pattern hair loss.[2]

The 2017 meta-analysis found 5 percent and 2 percent minoxidil in men and 2 percent in women superior to placebo, alongside 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser light.[4] A 2022 comparison ranked probable efficacy as dutasteride 0.5 mg, finasteride 5 mg, oral minoxidil 5 mg, finasteride 1 mg, then oral minoxidil 0.25 mg.[7] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies concluded many treatments promote hair growth and favoured an individualised, multifaceted approach.[15]

Human trials are extensive. Randomised trials include the 5 percent versus 2 percent versus placebo trial in men, a 2024 randomised trial of low-dose oral versus topical minoxidil, the 2024 JAMA Dermatology trial of oral versus topical minoxidil in men, a trial of 0.25 percent finasteride with 3 percent minoxidil versus minoxidil alone, and a trial comparing pumpkin seed oil with 5 percent minoxidil foam in female pattern hair loss.[14][16][6][17][18]

Registered studies include a phase 3 trial of 5 percent foam in 352 men with male pattern hair loss (NCT00151515), phase 3 trials in women (NCT01145625, n=322; NCT00958750, n=113), a microarray analysis of scalp biopsies after treatment (NCT01309191), and a topical finasteride-minoxidil combination study (NCT05990400).[19][20][21][22][23] A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology offers recommendations for safe and effective topical and oral use, and a 2025 article in PubMed Central reviews oral minoxidil in alopecia.[24][25]
An early 1987 review described minoxidil's use in male pattern alopecia and alopecia areata, and found side effects almost entirely cutaneous in patients without cardiovascular disease.[26]

Topical minoxidil is generally well tolerated; common effects are itching, local irritation and unwanted hair growth elsewhere, and alcohol and propylene glycol in some products may dry the scalp and cause dandruff or contact dermatitis.[1] Temporary shedding is described for both topical and oral forms.[1] The US label for a 5 percent product advises against use by women, people under 18, and those with a red, inflamed or irritated scalp.[10]

Side effects of oral minoxidil include salt and water retention with edema, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches and hypertrichosis.[1] Pericarditis, pericardial and pleural effusion and cardiac tamponade have been implicated, with pericardial effusion in about 3 percent at hypertension doses; Wikipedia says these are much less common at the low doses used for hair loss.[1] Absolute contraindications include pheochromocytoma, prior pericardial effusion or tamponade, and pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1] Low-dose oral minoxidil's effect on blood pressure is discussed on tressless.com.[27]

Wikipedia reports that aspirin may reduce topical minoxidil's effect by inhibiting the sulfotransferase that activates it, and that paracetamol and salicylic acid may similarly interfere.[1] It also describes a case of a seven-year-old who ingested a teaspoon of a minoxidil product and had hypotension and tachycardia for about 40 hours.[1]

The mechanism of hair growth is not fully understood.[1][28] Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by sulfotransferase (SULT1A1 in follicles) into minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels; reviews also describe vasodilator, anti-inflammatory, Wnt/beta-catenin-inducing and antiandrogen actions, and effects on the length of anagen and telogen phases.[1][2] Expression of SULT1A1 has been reported to predict response to topical minoxidil, so people with higher follicular sulfotransferase activity may respond better.[1][2] Growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and IGF-1 are induced in dermal papilla cells.[1]

Oral absorption is about 90 percent or more with peak levels in 30 to 60 minutes; only about 1.2 to 1.4 percent of topical minoxidil is absorbed through the scalp, with serum levels usually below 5 ng/mL.[1][2] Half-life is about 4 hours.[7]

Wikipedia dates minoxidil's discovery to 1963 and its introduction for hypertension to 1971, and says researchers unexpectedly found it causes hair growth, leading to repurposing as a topical hair-loss treatment.[1] A 2019 review notes that the discovery of hypertrichosis as a common side effect of the antihypertensive led to the topical formulation, and that it remains the mainstay treatment for androgenetic alopecia.[29] Grokipedia says Upjohn developed it and the US approved topical use for hair loss in 1988; this AI-generated source is attributed here.[9]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities
paras: Forums such as community.tressless.com and hairlosstalk.com host threads on oral minoxidil, including users announcing they are starting it, recommendations on oral dosage and sources, and a thread on low-dose oral minoxidil and blood pressure.[30][31][27] On T Nation, men discuss the Kirkland store brand, add low-dose oral minoxidil alongside testosterone, or ask whether Rogaine would affect natural status in competition; a user also says the drug has about 40 percent good responders on topical use.[32][33][34][35]

timeline.event: Introduced for treatment of high blood pressure.[1]
Early clinical review of topical minoxidil for male pattern alopecia published.[26]
Topical minoxidil approved for hair loss in the US, per Grokipedia.[9]
Randomised trial of 5 percent versus 2 percent topical minoxidil in men published.[14]
Meta-analysis supports 2 and 5 percent minoxidil over placebo.[4]
JAMA Dermatology trial compares oral and topical minoxidil in men.[6]
Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology publishes recommendations for topical and oral use.[24]

lore.intro: Minoxidil is discussed as the baseline growth treatment in hair-loss communities, with growing interest in low-dose oral use as an alternative to topical application.[30][31][36]

claims.claim: Minoxidil regrows and thickens hair independent of hormones
claims.believers: Users report using it alone or with finasteride and describe family members with good results.[34][8]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses show topical minoxidil beats placebo, though the effect depends on continued use.[4][1]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil works better than topical and is easier to stick with
claims.believers: Forum posters announce switching to oral minoxidil and trade views on dosing sources.[30][31]
claims.experts: A 2024 JAMA Dermatology trial and other randomised trials compared oral and topical forms; a review reports oral 5 mg more effective than topical at six months, but oral minoxidil is off-label and has cardiovascular effects.[6][16][2]

claims.claim: Low-dose oral minoxidil does not affect blood pressure
claims.believers: A tressless.com thread argues low-dose oral minoxidil does not significantly affect blood pressure.[27]
claims.experts: Reviews list hypotension, tachycardia and edema as dose-dependent oral effects, and Wikipedia says cardiovascular complications are rarer at low doses.[7][1]

claims.claim: Early shedding means it is working
claims.believers: Users describe an initial shedding phase before regrowth, consistent with community advice to be patient.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists temporary shedding as a known effect and explains minoxidil may push telogen follicles to shed before replacement by thicker hairs.[1]

claims.believers: Beard-growth use is widely discussed in appearance communities.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states minoxidil has been studied for beard growth, including in transgender men.[1]

claims.claim: Using minoxidil would disqualify someone as a natural lifter
claims.believers: One forum comment jokingly asks whether Rogaine would cost natural status.[35]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed do not describe minoxidil as an anabolic agent; it is a vasodilator used for hair loss.[1]
